subject: Science
source: National Curriculum KS1 Science (Plants; Seasonal changes); Drive Science folder 'Science lower school' (3.8 organisms) | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 8): Tarbiyyah Primary Year 1 curriculum map and Science Long Term Plan 2023-24 (Cornerstones Moon Zoom! and Rain & Sunrays), TGA Year 1 Curriculum Pack (Topic); home practicals with household items

lessons.title: Plants around us
objectives: Name some common garden and wild plants
Say the difference between a plant and an animal
Look carefully at a plant and describe it

keywords.def: a living thing that grows in soil and makes its own food
the part of a plant that is often colourful
a place where people grow plants
a plant that grows by itself without being planted

starter: Bismillah. Name two things that are alive.
What do animals need to stay alive?
Name one thing you can see in a garden.

teach.heading: What is a plant?
teach.note: Ask: 'Is a tree alive?' 'Can it run?' Establish plants are living but different from animals. Misconception: plants are not alive because they do not move.

teach.heading: Garden plants
bullets: Roses and daffodils are garden plants
Tomatoes and mint are garden plants
teach.note: Show clear photos. Ask 'Who plants these?' (people). Ask children what plants grow near their homes, including herbs and pot plants.

teach.heading: Wild plants
bullets: Daisies and dandelions are wild plants
Grass and moss are wild plants
teach.note: Show a daisy and a dandelion. Safe online task: children look from a window or garden. They must not pick or eat any wild plant, as some are harmful.

teach.heading: Looking closely
teach.note: Model a description: 'This leaf is green, long and thin.' Children describe a plant at home or a picture you show.

practice: Which is a garden plant: a rose or a dandelion growing in a crack?
Is a daisy alive? Tell your partner why.
Describe this picture of a leaf using colour, shape and size.
independent: Draw one garden plant and one wild plant. Label each with its name.
Write one sentence: 'A plant is a living thing because ...'
exit: Name one garden plant and one wild plant.
True or false: plants are alive.
lessons.homework: Draw a plant you can see at home or in a garden and write its name or colour.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a picture word bank (rose, daisy, grass, tree). Stretch: sort five plants into garden or wild and explain.

lessons.title: Parts of a plant
objectives: Name the roots, stem, leaf, flower and fruit
Say what each part does in simple words

keywords.def: the part under the soil that takes in water
the part that holds the plant up and carries water
the flat part that helps the plant make food
a coloured part of a flower

starter: Bismillah. Name one garden plant and one wild plant.
Is a plant alive? How do you know?

teach.heading: Under the ground: roots
bullets: Roots hold the plant in place
teach.note: Show a picture of a pulled-up plant with roots visible. Ask 'Why does a plant need roots?' Compare to feet that keep us standing.

teach.heading: Stem and leaves
bullets: The stem holds the plant up
teach.note: Hold up a real stem (celery, or a stem of mint) if available. Keep language simple: leaves use sunlight to make food for the plant. Do not teach photosynthesis detail yet.

teach.heading: Flower and fruit
teach.note: Safe demo: cut open an apple at home or on video to show seeds. A grown-up should do the cutting. Ask 'What could grow from a seed?'

teach.heading: Allah made plants
teach.note: Link to gratitude. Gently mention Qur'an 6:99 (Allah sends down water from the sky and brings out plants) in simple words: 'Allah sends rain so plants can grow.'

practice: Which part of the plant is under the soil?
Match the part to the job: roots, stem, leaf. Jobs: takes in water, holds the plant up, helps make food.
Label the diagram of a flower plant: root, stem, leaf, flower.
independent: Draw a plant and label four parts: root, stem, leaf, flower.
Complete the sentences: 'The roots take in ...' and 'The stem holds ...'
exit: Which part takes in water: root or flower?
Name two parts of a plant.
lessons.homework: Find a plant at home and point to its leaf and stem. Tell a grown-up what each part does.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use colour-coded labels and a real plant on camera. Stretch: explain what would happen to a plant with no roots.

lessons.title: Deciduous and evergreen trees
objectives: Name the parts of a tree: trunk, branch, leaf, root
Know that deciduous trees lose their leaves in autumn
Know that evergreen trees keep green leaves all year

keywords.def: the thick main stem of a tree
a tree that loses its leaves in autumn
a tree that keeps green leaves all year
an arm of a tree that grows from the trunk

starter: Bismillah. Which part of a plant is under the soil?
Name the season when leaves fall off.

teach.heading: Parts of a tree
bullets: It has roots under the ground
teach.note: Show a labelled tree. Ask children to point to each part. A tree is a big plant with a woody trunk.

teach.heading: Deciduous trees
bullets: Oak and horse chestnut are deciduous
Their leaves change colour in autumn
teach.note: Show photos of an oak in summer and in autumn. Say 'deciduous' together slowly. Explain the tree rests in winter.

teach.heading: Evergreen trees
teach.note: Show a pine tree photo. Misconception: evergreens never lose any leaves; they do lose some, but never all at once.

teach.heading: Sorting trees
bullets: Look at the leaves in autumn
teach.note: Give a quick sorting game with six pictures. Children say 'deciduous' or 'evergreen'. Safe task: observe from a window; no climbing or touching unknown plants.

practice: Is an oak tree deciduous or evergreen?
A tree has green leaves in January. Which type is it?
Point to the trunk on this tree picture.
independent: Draw two trees side by side: one deciduous in autumn and one evergreen. Label each.
Write the words 'deciduous' and 'evergreen' and say what each means.
exit: Which tree loses its leaves in autumn?
lessons.homework: Look at trees on the way out or from a window. Tell a grown-up if each one has green leaves or not.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use matching cards with pictures and the two key words. Stretch: explain why an evergreen looks green in winter.

lessons.title: Autumn becomes winter
objectives: Name the four seasons in order
Describe changes in weather and daylight from autumn to winter
Say how animals and people get ready for winter

keywords.def: one of four parts of the year: spring, summer, autumn, winter
the time when it is light outside
to sleep through the winter
how hot or cold something is

starter: Bismillah. Name a tree that loses its leaves in autumn.
Is it hot or cold in winter?

teach.heading: Four seasons
bullets: They happen in the same order
teach.note: Use a cycle picture. Children say the seasons in order, with actions. Ask which season we are in now (November: autumn, nearly winter).

teach.heading: Weather changes
bullets: There is more rain and wind
teach.note: Ask children to look at today's weather. Compare to summer using pictures. Frost: tiny ice crystals on cold mornings.

teach.heading: Shorter days
teach.note: Safe demo: use a torch and a child's toy to show light. In November the sun sets early in the UK. Ask 'When did it get dark last night?'

teach.heading: Getting ready for winter
bullets: Birds may fly to warmer places
teach.note: Hedgehogs hibernate. Many birds migrate. Ask children how their family gets ready (coats, heating). Note Islamic ethos: thank Allah for warm homes and think of those who need help.

practice: Say the four seasons in order.
Which is more likely in winter: frost or a heatwave?
Why might a hedgehog hibernate in winter?
independent: Draw a picture of an autumn day and a winter day. Write one word for the weather on each.
Write two things that change from autumn to winter.
exit: Are days longer or shorter in winter?
lessons.homework: Look outside each morning this week and write or draw the weather. Is it getting colder?
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a season picture strip with words; allow acting out. Stretch: explain why we cannot play outside as late in winter.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials (Moon Zoom! and Rain & Sunrays)
lessons.title: Object or material?
lessons.bigQuestion: What is a rocket made of?
objectives: To understand that every object is made from a material
successCriteria: All: name four materials: wood, plastic, glass, metal
Most: say what material an object is made from
Some: find one object made from two materials
lessons.crossCurricular: English: saying full sentences: 'It is made of ...'
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the materials Allah gave us

keywords.def: a thing you can see and touch
what a thing is made of
a material that comes from trees
a hard, shiny material, like a spoon
a material made in factories, used for bottles
a see-through material, used for windows

hook.text: A spoon and a fork are different objects. Can they be made of the same thing?

islamicLink.text: Allah made the world and everything in it. He made trees, rocks, water and metals for us to use. Allah says He sent down iron, which has many benefits for people (al-Hadid 57:25). We say alhamdulillah for the things we use every day.

starter.q: What do we call the big round thing in the night sky?
Name one thing in your bedroom.
starter.a: For example: a bed, a lamp, a book

teach.heading: Objects and materials
bullets: A material is what it is made of
A cup is an object; it can be glass or plastic
teach.note: Hold up a metal spoon. Say: this is an object. It is a spoon. It is made of metal. Metal is the material. Ask pupils to hold up one object near them.

teach.heading: Wood and metal
bullets: Metal is hard and often shiny
A rocket is made mostly of metal
teach.note: Show a wooden spoon and a metal spoon. Ask: how are they the same? How are they different? Rockets need strong metal to fly to space.

teach.heading: Plastic, glass, rock and water
teach.note: The Moon is made of rock. Astronauts brought Moon rock back to Earth. Water is a material too: it is in our cups and in the sea.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: A window is made of which material?
check.why: Windows are glass so we can see through them. Wood and rock are not see-through.

practice.q: What material is a metal spoon made of?
practice.model:
Look at the object.
It is a spoon.
It is hard and shiny.
It is made of metal.

practice.q: What material is a window made of?
What material is a pencil made of?

independent.q: Core: Material hunt. Find one object made of wood, metal, plastic and glass. Show each one to the camera.
independent.a: For example: wooden spoon, metal key, plastic bottle, glass jar
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: I found a jar. It is made of glass. I put it on the glass card.

independent.q: Extend: Find an object made of rock or stone.
independent.a: For example: a pebble or a stone step

independent.q: Stretch: Find one object made of two materials.
independent.a: For example: a pencil (wood and graphite) or a chair (wood and metal)

exit.q: Big question: what is a rocket made of?
exit.a: Mostly metal, because metal is strong

lessons.homework: Material hunt at home: find one object made of each of six materials (wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, rock) and tell an adult.
lessons.send: SEND: real objects to hold and picture cards of the six materials. EAL: say 'It is made of ...' with each object. Stretch: sort objects made of two materials.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials (Moon Zoom! and Rain & Sunrays)
lessons.title: Hard or soft, bendy or stiff?
lessons.bigQuestion: Which material would you choose for a window, and why?
objectives: To understand that materials have properties we can test by touch and sight
successCriteria: All: say if a material is hard or soft
Most: sort objects by one property
Some: say if a material is see-through or not
lessons.smsc: Moral: handling objects carefully and safely at home

keywords.def: what a material is like
does not squash when you press it
squashes when you press it
bends easily
you can see through it
you cannot see through it

hook.text: Why is a window not made of wood?

islamicLink.text: Allah made each material different. Some are hard like rock and some are soft like wool. Allah says He made for us from the wool of animals things we use and enjoy (an-Nahl 16:80). Choosing the right material is using Allah's gifts wisely.

starter.q: What material is a spoon often made of?
Name a material that comes from trees.
A bottle is often made of:

teach.heading: What is a property?
bullets: A property tells us what a material is like
teach.note: Press a sponge, then a stone. Ask: which squashed? The sponge is soft. The stone is hard. Hard and soft are properties.

teach.heading: Can we see through it?
bullets: Transparent: we can see through it
Opaque: we cannot see through it
Glass is transparent; wood is opaque
teach.note: Hold a glass jar and a wooden board in front of a toy. Ask: can you see the toy?

teach.heading: Sort them
bullets: Put each one in a group
teach.note: Pupils call out the letter and group. Bend gently; never bend glass.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results and ask one pupil why.

check.why: A cushion squashes when pressed. A brick and a pan are hard.

practice.q: Is a sponge hard or soft?
practice.model:
Press it.
It squashes.
So it is soft.

practice.q: Is a metal spoon bendy or stiff?
Can you see through cling film?

independent.q: Core: Find four objects at home. Show each one and say 'hard' or 'soft'.
independent.a: For example: book hard, sock soft, cup hard, towel soft
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: this is a towel. I press it. It squashes. It is soft.

independent.q: Extend: Which of your objects is bendy?
independent.a: For example: a sock, a plastic ruler, a rubber band

independent.q: Stretch: Why is a window made of glass and not wood?
independent.a: Glass is transparent, so light comes in and we can see out

exit.q: Big question: which material would you choose for a window, and why?
exit.a: Glass, because it is transparent and hard

lessons.homework: Hold four objects up to a lamp or window with an adult: which ones let light through?
lessons.send: SEND: feel-and-say with a real sponge and stone; picture cards for hard and soft. EAL: hard, soft, bendy, see-through with actions. Stretch: describe one object with two properties.

Property picture cards: hard, soft, bendy, stiff, transparent, opaque (portal printable)
Household items: sponge, stone, metal spoon, cushion, cling film, wooden block

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials (Moon Zoom! and Rain & Sunrays)
lessons.title: Which fabric would make a good rain hat?
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we find out which fabric keeps rain out?
objectives: To understand how a simple test can show which material is waterproof
successCriteria: Most: predict which fabric will keep water out
Some: say how to keep the test fair
lessons.smsc: Social: working safely with an adult helper

keywords.def: does not let water through
soaks up water
a soft material made for clothes
a way to find something out
say what you think will happen

hook.text: Why do people wear a raincoat and not a towel when it rains?

islamicLink.text: Rain is a mercy from Allah. Allah says He sends down blessed rain from the sky and grows gardens with it (Qaf 50:9). We thank Allah for rain, and we choose clothes that keep us dry and warm.

starter.q: Is a sponge hard or soft?
Name one material that is opaque.

teach.heading: Waterproof or absorbent?
teach.note: Drip water on a plastic bag and on kitchen roll. Ask: what happened to the water on each?

teach.heading: Our test
bullets: Drip 5 spoons of water on top
teach.note: Model it slowly with an elastic band holding the fabric. Say: same cup, same water, same number of spoons for every fabric.

teach.heading: Keep it fair
teach.note: Ask: if I pour a jug on one and one spoon on another, is that fair? No.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results; ask why.

check.q: Which would make the best rain hat?
check.why: Plastic is waterproof. Kitchen roll and cotton soak up water.

practice.q: Predict: will water go through kitchen roll?
practice.model:
Kitchen roll soaks up water.
So water will go through.
I predict the cup will be wet.

practice.q: Predict: will water go through foil?
Why do we use 5 spoons of water every time?

independent.q: Core: With an adult, test three fabrics over a cup (a plastic bag, kitchen roll, an old sock). Put a tick if the cup stays dry.
independent.a: Plastic bag: tick (dry); kitchen roll: cross (wet); sock: cross (wet)
independent.model: Teacher shows it first with foil: foil on the cup, 5 spoons of water, wait, look. The cup is dry. Tick.

independent.q: Extend: Which fabric was best for a rain hat?
independent.a: The plastic bag, because it is waterproof

independent.q: Stretch: What one thing did you change in the test?

exit.a: B) water does not go through

exit.q: Big question: how can we find out which fabric keeps rain out?
exit.a: Drip the same water on each fabric over a cup and see which cup stays dry

lessons.homework: Drip water on four household materials with an adult and record which let water through.
lessons.send: SEND: adult helper drips the water; tick or cross cards. EAL: wet, dry, waterproof with pictures. Stretch: test a fourth fabric and explain the result.

Results table: tick or cross for three fabrics (portal printable)

Fabrics: a plastic bag (adult only, keep away from faces), kitchen roll, an old sock, foil

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials (Moon Zoom! and Rain & Sunrays)
lessons.title: Winter weather and short days
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is it dark when we eat dinner in winter?
objectives: To understand that winter has cold weather and short days
successCriteria: All: name two kinds of winter weather
Most: say that winter days are short
Some: say that the sun sets a little later each day after winter starts
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: telling the time to the hour for sunset
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: noticing the signs of Allah in the seasons

keywords.def: the coldest season of the year
what it is like outside: sun, rain, wind
the time when the Sun lights the sky
when the Sun goes down
one of four parts of the year

hook.text: Is it light or dark when you wake up in January? What about July?

islamicLink.text: Allah made the seasons and the night and the day. Allah says that in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the changing of night and day there are signs for people who think (Al Imran 3:190). Short winter days remind us of Allah's perfect plan. We pray Maghrib after sunset, so in winter Maghrib comes early.

starter.q: Is a towel waterproof or absorbent?

teach.heading: The four seasons
bullets: January and February are in winter
Each season has its own weather
teach.note: Say the seasons in order together. Ask: which season are we in now?

teach.heading: Winter weather
bullets: We wear coats, hats and gloves
teach.note: Look out of the window together. Ask: what is the weather today? What are you wearing to go out?

teach.heading: Short days
bullets: In summer the Sun sets late
teach.note: In London in late December the Sun is up for about 8 hours. In June it is up for about 16 hours.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: Winter days are short. They are not always sunny: winter brings rain, wind and frost.

practice.q: Name two kinds of winter weather.
practice.a: For example: frost and rain, or snow and wind
practice.model:
Look outside.
It is cold.
There is frost on the grass.
Frost and wind are winter weather.

practice.q: Are winter days long or short?
What do we wear in winter to keep warm?
practice.a: For example: a coat, hat, gloves, scarf

independent.q: Core: Start your weather diary. Draw today's weather and write one word.
independent.a: For example: a cloud and the word 'cloudy'
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: I look out. It is grey and wet. I draw a cloud with rain. I write 'rainy'.

independent.q: Extend: Ask an adult what time the Sun will set today.
independent.a: About 4 to 5 o'clock in January and early February in the UK

independent.q: Stretch: Is the sunset earlier or later than last week?
independent.a: A little later, because the days are getting longer after winter begins

exit.q: Big question: why is it dark when we eat dinner in winter?
exit.a: Because winter days are short and the Sun sets early

lessons.homework: Record the weather and the sunset time each day for one week in your weather diary.
lessons.send: SEND: weather picture symbols to stick in the diary. EAL: sunny, rainy, windy, cold with pictures. Stretch: compare the sunset time on Monday and Friday.
